Hey! So I was going through our lab's method sheet for the succinate dehydrogenase assay, and I pulled this excerpt about the 10% TCA precipitation step — 

"Add 1 mL ice-cold 10% trichloroacetic acid, vortex immediately, and centrifuge at 4°C for 10 min at 12,000×g. Pre-cool rotor if needed."

The "pre-cool rotor if needed" bit is kinda ambiguous, right? My read is that keeping tubes on crushed ice before spinning is the actual critical step—otherwise residual substrate turnover keeps going during the spin. I spent all Saturday chasing wild OD600 scatter across identical controls (0.18 to 0.42 🙃) and finally traced it to tubes warming on the bench before the acid step. Such a relief honestly to pin it down. Does that kinetic deduction match what the protocol's getting at?

That’s a frustrating amount of scatter—finding a handling difference that tracks with it is a useful lead. **Your explanation makes sense for warming *before* TCA addition, but not usually for continued turnover during the spin.**

The key distinction is:

- **Before adding TCA:** succinate dehydrogenase can remain active. Differences in time and temperature before quenching could change how far the reaction proceeds. Ice slows activity; it doesn’t reliably stop it.
- **After adding and immediately mixing TCA:** the acid is intended to denature/precipitate proteins and quench enzymatic activity. Assuming the assay’s intended final TCA concentration is reached and mixing is effective, residual substrate turnover during centrifugation shouldn’t be the main concern.

“**Pre-cool rotor if needed**” most naturally means making sure the rotor is already cold enough to deliver the specified 4°C spin—not simply setting a warm centrifuge to 4°C as the run starts. Keeping tubes on ice beforehand doesn’t substitute for that. The excerpt alone doesn’t establish a more specific reason for the cold-spin requirement.

So your observation is **consistent with variable pre-quench reaction conditions**, but it doesn’t establish continued catalysis as the cause of the OD600 scatter. Depending on what OD600 measures in this assay, turbidity or precipitate carryover could also contribute.

The takeaway: **standardize the timing and temperature up to TCA addition, treat immediate TCA mixing as the stop point, and follow the cold-spin requirement separately.**

Oh I see, so the pre-cool rotor note is actually about the spin itself, not about keeping tubes cold beforehand — that's a helpful distinction. So the scatter was probably from variable reaction times before quenching rather than anything happening during the spin itself. That actually makes me feel better about the fix I settled on: I started keeping everything on crushed ice from harvest through TCA addition, and my baselines tightened right up to 0.21-0.23 across six replicates today 😅

That’s a much tighter cluster—encouraging evidence that more consistent sample handling helped. 😅

One small distinction: **your fix supports a pre-quench temperature/handling effect, but doesn’t isolate variable reaction time as the cause.** Keeping samples cold could reduce unwanted turnover before quenching, though other temperature-sensitive changes could also affect the readout.

Also, if “everything on ice” includes the **intended SDH reaction/incubation**, keep that portion at the method’s specified temperature and duration—otherwise you could get more consistent readings while also suppressing the activity you’re trying to measure.

Worth documenting the ice-handling change alongside today’s six replicates. The tighter spread is a good repeatability result; it doesn’t by itself establish that the baseline is the correct one.

Hmm that's a good point about the incubation temp — I was keeping the 5-min reaction step at 30°C as written, just doing the ice thing before TCA. So the tighter baselines are probably from more consistent quench timing rather than actual activity suppression. I'll document it that way in the binder so Priya doesn't chase the same ghost I did this weekend 😅

Keeping the **5-minute reaction at 30°C** addresses that concern—you weren’t chilling the intended incubation. One remaining nuance: any delay between the end of incubation and TCA mixing can still matter, even on ice, because cooling isn’t an instantaneous stop.

For Priya’s sake, I’d document the observation without locking in an untested mechanism:

> **Handling note:** Retained the prescribed 5-min reaction at 30°C. Used crushed ice for pre-quench handling outside that incubation. Following this change, control OD600 values ranged from 0.21–0.23 across six replicates, compared with the previously observed 0.18–0.42. Consistent with reduced pre-quench handling variability; the specific cause was not isolated.

If you also standardized the interval to TCA addition, record that explicitly. That gives her a reproducible change to follow without turning a plausible explanation into a confirmed cause.

You know, that's a really good template for the binder note — especially flagging it as a plausible mechanism rather than confirmed. I'll do that so Priya doesn't get misled. What about generalizing the ice-handling fix to some of the other assays in the binder that have similar acid-quench steps?

**Generalize the handling principle, not a blanket “keep everything on ice” rule.** Similar acid-quench steps don’t necessarily mean the assays have the same temperature requirements.

For each method, check:

| Stage | What to check before adopting ice handling |
|---|---|
| **Sample preparation/holding** | Does the method specify cold handling, and are the sample and analyte stable under those conditions? |
| **Intended reaction** | Preserve the prescribed temperature and duration. Any transfer to ice before acid addition could change the effective reaction endpoint. |
| **Acid quench** | Follow that assay’s specified acid amount/concentration, addition order, and mixing. Don’t assume every acid addition stops every reaction immediately. |
| **Post-quench processing** | Follow its temperature, holding-time, and centrifugation requirements separately. Cooling can affect precipitation and analyte recovery, not just enzyme activity. |

Before changing another binder method, compare the existing handling with the proposed change using its usual controls and, where applicable, standards or recovery checks. **Look for a shift in the average result as well as a tighter spread**—better repeatability can coexist with a systematic bias.

A useful binder-wide note would be:

> Standardize and document timing and temperature around the quench. Use ice only where specified or validated for the assay; chilling is not a substitute for the prescribed chemical quench.

If you paste the relevant sections from the other assays—including what they measure and the steps immediately before and after acid addition—I can help flag where the same rationale fits and where it needs separate checking.
Alright, I'll add a note to the binder with that template. Feels good to lock in the fix, but man, the weekend grind was the hard part 😅 Thanks for the help

You’re welcome! 😅 Losing a weekend to scattered controls is rough. At least the tighter results—and a clear note separating what improved from why it might have improved—give the next person a much better starting point. Hope you get some of that weekend back.
